1.title: The Chain of the Revelation
1.context: The book opens by tracing its own delivery: God gave the revelation to Jesus Christ, who sent his angel to his servant John, who bore witness to everything he saw. What must soon take place is shown, not hidden.
1.question: What has God made known to you through a chain of faithful hands?

1.title: Blessed Are Those Who Hear and Obey
1.context: The first of the book's seven blessings rests on the reader, the hearers, and those who obey what is written, because the time is near. The blessing is on response, not curiosity alone.
1.question: What would obeying, not just hearing, look like for one thing you already know?

1.title: Grace and Peace, and Released by His Blood
1.context: The letter greets seven real churches in Asia from the God who is and was and is to come, from the seven Spirits before his throne, and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead. The greeting rises into praise: he loves us, has released us from our sins by his blood, and made us a kingdom and priests. This is the reader's identity before any vision begins.
1.question: What does it mean for you that release came by his blood, not your effort?

1.title: Every Eye Will See Him
1.context: He comes with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him. The Alpha and the Omega speaks the book's last word in advance: I am who is and was and is to come, the Almighty.
1.question: How does knowing the end change how you read everything between?

2.title: Your Brother and Partner in Tribulation
2.context: John introduces himself not by office but by kinship: your brother and partner in the tribulation, kingdom, and perseverance in Jesus, exiled on Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.
2.question: Who has been a partner with you in perseverance, not just in success?

2.title: Write on a Scroll What You See
2.context: On the Lord's day, in the Spirit, John hears a loud voice like a trumpet commissioning the book: write what you see and send it to the seven churches, real congregations then living in Asia.
2.question: What have you been given to record faithfully rather than explain away?

2.title: One Like a Son of Man
2.context: Among seven golden lampstands stands one like a son of man, robed to the feet with a golden sash, hair white as wool and snow, eyes like flame, feet like burnished bronze, voice like many waters, face like the sun in full strength.
2.question: Which detail of this portrait do you most need to remember today?

2.title: Do Not Be Afraid
2.context: John falls at his feet as dead, and the hand that holds the seven stars touches him: Do not be afraid. I am the First and the Last and the Living One; I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, holding the keys of death and Hades.
2.question: What fear needs to hear that the Living One holds the keys?

2.title: The Mystery Explained
2.context: The book interprets its own first symbols: the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the churches themselves. Where the book explains, the telling uses its explanation.
2.question: Where has God already explained more than you have been willing to receive?

3.title: Ephesus: Deeds, Toil, Perseverance
3.context: Each letter opens from a feature of the opening vision. Ephesus hears real commendation: deeds, toil, perseverance, intolerance of evil, tested claims, and hatred of the Nicolaitans' practices. The reflection on the letters' shared shape rides this scene.
3.question: What perseverance in your life deserves to be named and kept?

3.title: You Have Left Your First Love
3.context: Against all that orthodoxy stands one charge: the first love is gone. The remedy is as concrete as the charge: remember, repent, and do the deeds you did at first, or the lampstand itself is removed.
3.question: What deed from your first love could you simply do again this week?

3.title: Smyrna: Be Faithful unto Death
3.context: Smyrna receives no rebuke. Poor in goods and rich in fact, slandered and facing prison and ten days of tribulation, it is promised that the second death will not hurt those who overcome.
3.question: What would faithfulness look like if the outcome were not yours to control?

4.title: Pergamum: Where Satan's Throne Is
4.context: Pergamum hears from the one with the sharp two-edged sword. Its people dwell where Satan's throne is, an imperial cult center, yet hold fast the name and did not deny the faith even when Antipas was put to death among them.
4.question: Where do you live and work that holding fast costs something real?

4.title: Some Hold the Teaching of Balaam
4.context: The charge is compromise: some eat food sacrificed to idols and practice sexual immorality after Balaam's pattern. The promise to the overcomer is hidden manna and a white stone with a new name known only to its receiver.
4.question: What compromise have you been calling it wisdom to tolerate?

4.title: Thyatira: Love, Faith, Service
4.context: The longest letter opens with the fullest description, the Son of God with eyes like flame, and commends deeds, love, faith, service, and perseverance, with later works greater than the first.
4.question: Are your later works greater than your first, and what would make them so?

4.title: You Tolerate That Woman Jezebel
4.context: The letter applies the name Jezebel to a teacher in Thyatira who calls herself a prophetess; she was given time to repent and refused. Those who hold to what they have are told only to hold fast until he comes.
4.question: Where has tolerance stopped being love and become surrender?

4.title: I Will Give Him the Morning Star
4.context: The overcomer who keeps the deeds to the end receives authority over the nations, shepherding with a rod of iron in the words of Psalm 2, and the morning star itself from the one who gives it.
4.question: What are you keeping, steadily, that is worth keeping to the end?

5.title: Sardis: A Name for Being Alive
5.context: Sardis has the reputation of being alive and is dead: works incomplete, watchfulness gone, garments soiled. The call is to wake up, strengthen what remains, remember what was received, and repent.
5.question: Where has your reputation outrun your reality, and what is the first act of waking?

5.title: A Few Names Who Have Not Soiled Their Garments
5.context: Even in Sardis a few kept their garments clean; they will walk with him in white. The overcomer's name will never be blotted from the book of life, and will be confessed before the Father and his angels.
5.question: Whose quiet faithfulness around you deserves to be honored by name?

5.title: Philadelphia: An Open Door
5.context: Philadelphia receives no rebuke. The Holy One, the True One, who holds the key of David, has set before this little-strength church an open door no one can shut, because it kept his word and did not deny his name.
5.question: What open door in front of you is small enough to walk through humbly?

5.title: Hold Fast What You Have
5.context: The overcomer becomes a pillar in God's temple, never to leave it, bearing three names: God's, the new Jerusalem's, and Christ's own new name. The reflection on this church's opponents rides this scene.
5.question: What do you need to hold fast so that no one takes your crown?

6.title: Laodicea: The Amen, the Faithful and True Witness
6.context: The last letter opens with the strangest titles: the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the Originator of God's creation, in the BSB's wording. Laodicea was wealthy in banking, medicine, and black wool, and proud of all three.
6.question: How does Christ introduce himself to a church that thinks it needs nothing?

6.title: Neither Cold nor Hot
6.context: The charge is a temperature: works neither cold nor hot, lukewarm, nauseating to the speaker who would rather have either extreme. There is no praise in this letter at all.
6.question: Where have you settled for a temperature that costs nothing?

6.title: You Do Not Realize That You Are Wretched
6.context: The root is a false ledger: the church says rich and in need of nothing, and does not know it is wretched, pitiful, poor, blind, and naked. Self-deception, not persecution, is this church's danger.
6.question: What does your ledger say that heaven's ledger contradicts?

6.title: Buy from Me Gold Refined by Fire
6.context: The counsel answers each pride from the city's own industries: gold refined by fire for its poverty, white garments for its shame, salve for its blindness. Those he loves, he rebukes and disciplines; be earnest, then, and repent.
6.question: Which of your strengths has become the place you most need his supply?

6.title: Behold, I Stand at the Door and Knock
6.context: The picture the letters close with: Christ outside his own church's door, knocking, promising to come in and dine with anyone who hears and opens. The overcomer will sit with him on his throne.
6.question: What door of your life is he knocking at, and what would opening it today mean?

7.title: A Door Standing Open in Heaven
7.context: After the letters, the vision opens upward: a door standing open in heaven, the trumpet voice calling John up, and a throne set in heaven with one seated on it, jasper and carnelian in appearance, ringed by an emerald rainbow.
7.question: When did you last stop managing earth long enough to look at the throne?

7.title: Around the Throne
7.context: Twenty-four elders sit on thrones in white with golden crowns; lightning, rumblings, and thunder proceed from the center; seven lamps of fire burn; and a sea of glass like crystal spreads before the throne.
7.question: What in your life is currently arranged around the throne, and what is arranged around you?

7.title: Holy, Holy, Holy
7.context: Closest to the center, the four living creatures, covered with eyes and winged like the seraphim of Isaiah, never cease saying: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Almighty, who was, and is, and is to come.
7.question: What would your worship sound like if it never had to stop?

7.title: They Cast Their Crowns Before the Throne
7.context: Whenever the creatures give glory, the elders fall down and cast their crowns before the throne, declaring the one seated worthy, since by his will all things were created and have their being.
7.question: What crown of yours is ready to be cast down gladly?

8.title: The Scroll Sealed with Seven Seals
8.context: In the right hand of the one on the throne sits a scroll written inside and on the back, sealed with seven seals, and a mighty angel asks with a loud voice who is worthy to open it. Heaven's history waits on an answer.
8.question: What in your life feels sealed until the worthy one opens it?

8.title: Weep No More: The Lion Has Conquered
8.context: No one in heaven, on earth, or under the earth is found worthy, and John weeps loudly, until one elder answers the grief: the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered and can open the scroll.
8.question: Where do you need to hear weep no more from someone who can see farther than you?

8.title: A Lamb Who Appeared to Have Been Slain
8.context: John looks for the announced Lion and sees a Lamb standing, as though slain, with seven horns and seven eyes, who comes and takes the scroll from the right hand of the one seated. Announcement and sight are both kept, exactly as given.
8.question: Where has God answered you in a form you were not looking for?

8.title: You Were Slain, and by Your Blood You Ransomed People
8.context: The elders fall with harps and golden bowls of incense, which the verse itself names as the prayers of the saints, and sing a new song: ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, made a kingdom and priests.
8.question: Whose prayers, besides your own, are carried in those bowls?

8.title: To Him Who Sits on the Throne and to the Lamb
8.context: Myriads of angels take up the song, then every creature in heaven and earth and sea, and the elders fall down and worship as Amen confirms the whole creation's blessing, honor, glory, and might forever.
8.question: What would change if your worship joined a choir that size on purpose?

9.title: Come: The White Horse
9.context: The Lamb opens the seals and the four living creatures summon the riders one by one with a single word. The frame of the whole chapter, each seal opened by the Lamb himself, rides this scene.
9.question: What does it change for you that the seals are opened by the Lamb, not by chaos?

9.title: The Red Horse: Peace Taken from the Earth
9.context: The second rider is permitted to take peace from the earth so that people slay one another, and a great sword is given to him. War opens the series' second act.
9.question: Where do you need to be a peacemaker in a world licensed to slay itself?

9.title: The Black Horse: A Quart of Wheat for a Denarius
9.context: The third rider holds scales, and a voice prices the famine: a day's wage for a day's bread, with the oil and the wine spared. Luxury untouched while staples fail is part of the picture as given.
9.question: How do you hold what you have when others cannot buy bread?

9.title: The Pale Green Horse: Death, and Hades Behind Him
9.context: The fourth rider is named Death, with Hades following, and authority is given them over a fourth of the earth, by sword, famine, plague, and the beasts of the earth, in the pattern of older prophecies.
9.question: What does this sober picture ask of your courage rather than your fear?

10.title: How Long, O Lord
10.context: Under the altar, the souls of those slain for the word of God and their testimony cry out with the psalms' own question: how long until you judge and avenge? Martyrdom, not conquest, opens the fifth seal.
10.question: What prayer of how long do you need to pray honestly instead of politely?

10.title: White Robes, and Rest a Little Longer
10.context: The answer is a white robe and a wait: rest until the number of fellow servants to be killed is complete. Heaven's timetable includes a number the martyrs themselves must wait for.
10.question: Where is rest itself the obedience you are being given right now?

10.title: The Sun Became Black as Sackcloth
10.context: The sixth seal shakes everything: a great earthquake, the sun black as sackcloth, the moon like blood, stars falling like figs, the sky rolled up like a scroll, every mountain and island moved from its place.
10.question: What in your life is built on ground you assume cannot move?

10.title: Hide Us from the Wrath of the Lamb
10.context: From kings to slaves, everyone hides in caves calling on the mountains to fall on them, to hide them from the face of the one on the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day has come, and who can stand?
10.question: Who can stand is the question the next chapter exists to answer; where do you need to be found standing?

11.title: Do Not Harm Until We Have Sealed
11.context: Four angels hold back the four winds while another ascends from the sunrise with the seal of the living God, ordering the pause: no harm to earth, sea, or trees until God's servants are sealed on their foreheads.
11.question: Where might God's pause be protection you have been reading as delay?

11.title: 144,000 Sealed from Every Tribe
11.context: John hears the number, 144,000, twelve thousand from each of the twelve tribes, listed by name with Dan unnamed and Manasseh named, a fact the telling notes without explaining. Readers have long disagreed on who the 144,000 are; the telling names the disagreement and takes no side.
11.question: How do you hold a passage faithfully when faithful readers disagree about it?

11.title: A Multitude No One Could Count
11.context: What John sees next cannot be counted: a great multitude from every nation, tribe, people, and language, standing in white robes with palm branches, crying that salvation belongs to God and the Lamb. Heard, then seen: the pattern of the chapter.
11.question: Who do you expect to be surprised to stand beside in that crowd?

11.title: They Have Washed Their Robes in the Blood of the Lamb
11.context: An elder tests the seer and then teaches him: these are the ones coming out of the great tribulation, whose robes are white because they were washed in the Lamb's blood.
11.question: What in your life is clean only because it was washed, not because it was kept?

11.title: The Lamb Will Shepherd Them
11.context: Their future is told in older prophets' words: no hunger, no thirst, no scorching sun, springs of living water, and God wiping every tear, because the Lamb in the center of the throne will shepherd them himself.
11.question: Which of those nevers do you most need to hear as a promise today?

12.title: Silence in Heaven for Half an Hour
12.context: The seventh seal opens into heaven's most startling sound: silence for about half an hour. Then seven angels standing before God are given seven trumpets, and the judgments wait on something else first.
12.question: When has silence, not noise, been the sign that something weighty was coming?

12.title: The Prayers of All the Saints on the Golden Altar
12.context: Before any trumpet, prayer takes the stage: an angel offers much incense with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar, then hurls altar fire to the earth amid thunder, rumblings, lightning, and an earthquake.
12.question: Do you believe your prayers reach an altar before history moves? What follows from believing it?

12.title: The First and Second Trumpets
12.context: The trumpets strike in thirds: hail and fire mixed with blood burn a third of the earth and trees and all green grass; then something like a great mountain burning is thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea turns to blood.
12.question: What does the measured third, not everything, tell you about the Judge?

12.title: Wormwood
12.context: At the third trumpet a great star burning like a torch falls on a third of the rivers and springs. Its name is Wormwood, bitterness itself, and many die from the waters it poisons.
12.question: What bitterness have you let fall into your own springs, and what would cleansing require?

12.title: Woe, Woe, Woe
12.context: The fourth trumpet darkens a third of sun, moon, and stars, and over the darkened earth a single eagle cries with a loud voice: woe, woe, woe, for the trumpets still to come. Three woes are announced; none is softened.
12.question: Where do you need to hear a warning as mercy rather than as threat?

13.title: The Shaft of the Bottomless Pit
13.context: The fifth trumpet opens the earth downward: a star fallen from heaven receives the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit, and smoke like a great furnace darkens the sun and air as locusts come out onto the earth.
13.question: What locked things in your own life are you grateful stay locked?

13.title: They Were Told Not to Harm the Grass
13.context: The locusts carry limits as precise as the trumpets' thirds: no grass, no plant, no tree, only those without God's seal, and torment for five months, like a scorpion's sting, with death fleeing from those who seek it.
13.question: Where do stated limits on evil, even strange ones, steady your trust?

13.title: Abaddon, Apollyon
13.context: Their appearance is assembled from armies and animals: horses prepared for battle, gold-like crowns, human faces, women's hair, lions' teeth, iron breastplates, wings like chariots, and the angel of the bottomless pit as king, Destroyer in both tongues.
13.question: How do you describe something for which your world has no single picture?

13.title: The Four Angels Bound at the Euphrates
13.context: The sixth trumpet releases what the fifth only swarmed: four angels bound at the great river Euphrates, prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year, to kill a third of mankind.
13.question: What does the terrible precision of that appointment say about who governs history?

13.title: Two Hundred Million
13.context: The mounted troops number two hundred million, heard, not counted. Their horses kill from both ends, heads like lions breathing fire, smoke, and sulfur, tails like serpents with heads that injure.
13.question: When numbers overwhelm, what do you hold onto that cannot be outnumbered?

13.title: The Rest Did Not Repent
13.context: The chapter lands its bleakest sentence: those not killed did not repent of the works of their hands, their idols of gold and silver, their murders, sorceries, sexual immorality, or thefts. Survival itself did not teach them.
13.question: What have you survived that still has not taught you what it should?

14.title: A Mighty Angel with a Small Scroll
14.context: Between the trumpets the vision pauses on a mighty angel coming down robed in cloud, rainbow over his head, face like the sun, legs like pillars of fire, one foot on the sea and one on the land, holding a small scroll lying open.
14.question: Where do small, open things deserve more attention than the loud judgments around them?

14.title: Seal Up What the Seven Thunders Said
14.context: The angel cries out like a lion's roar and seven thunders answer, and John, about to write, is told to seal it up: the book that commissions writing also forbids it here, and the telling keeps the seal.
14.question: What are you content to leave sealed, trusting the one who spoke it?

14.title: There Will Be No More Delay
14.context: The angel raises his hand to heaven and swears by the one who lives forever, creator of all: there will be no more delay, and in the seventh trumpet's days the mystery of God will be fulfilled, as he announced to the prophets.
14.question: Where is no more delay good news for you, and where is it a warning?

14.title: Sweet in the Mouth, Bitter in the Belly
14.context: John takes and eats the small scroll on Ezekiel's pattern: sweet as honey in the mouth, bitter in the belly, and the commission is renewed in the same breath: you must prophesy again about many peoples and nations and kings.
14.question: What truth has been sweet to receive and bitter to carry?

15.title: Measure the Temple of God
15.context: John is given a measuring rod like a staff and told to measure the temple, the altar, and the worshipers, but to leave the outer court unmeasured, given to the nations who will trample the holy city for forty-two months.
15.question: What in the life of faith is measured and kept, even while much is trampled?

15.title: My Two Witnesses
15.context: For 1,260 days two witnesses prophesy in sackcloth, the two olive trees and two lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth, with fire for their enemies and power over rain, waters, and plagues, in the patterns of Moses and Elijah.
15.question: What would sackcloth witness look like in your place and time?

15.title: Their Dead Bodies Will Lie in the Street
15.context: When their testimony finishes, protection ends by design: the beast from the bottomless pit kills them, and their bodies lie three and a half days in the street of the great city, figuratively called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified, while the earth celebrates.
15.question: Where have you seen the world celebrate what it should have mourned?

15.title: Come Up Here
15.context: After three and a half days the breath of life from God enters them, they stand on their feet in great fear among the watchers, and a loud voice calls them up into heaven in a cloud while their enemies watch. The second woe ends under a great earthquake.
15.question: What testimony of yours looks finished that God may only be pausing?

15.title: The Kingdom of the World Has Become the Kingdom of Our Lord
15.context: The seventh trumpet sounds the book's great announcement: the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever. The elders worship, and the opened temple reveals the ark of his covenant.
15.question: What would you do today if you read that announcement as already true?

16.title: A Woman Clothed with the Sun
16.context: The sequence of seals and trumpets stops for a great sign: a woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet, a crown of twelve stars, crying out in the pains of childbirth. Who the woman is, readers have long read more than one way; the telling keeps the sign as shown.
16.question: Where do you need to trust a sign whose full meaning is larger than you?

16.title: A Huge Red Dragon
16.context: The second sign is her enemy: a huge red dragon with seven heads, ten horns, and seven crowns, whose tail sweeps a third of the stars to earth, standing before the woman to devour her child at birth.
16.question: What in your life waits to devour good things at their birth, and how will you guard them?

16.title: Caught Up to God and His Throne
16.context: The birth happens in two swift strokes: a son who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, caught up to God and his throne, and the woman fleeing into a wilderness place prepared by God, nourished there 1,260 days.
16.question: Where has God prepared a wilderness that turned out to be protection?

16.title: Michael and His Angels Fought the Dragon
16.context: Then war in heaven: Michael and his angels fight the dragon, who loses and is thrown down to earth with his angels, named in full as the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world, given no place in heaven any longer.
16.question: What does it mean that the accuser's eviction is heaven's fact before it is earth's experience?

16.title: They Conquered by the Blood of the Lamb
16.context: Heaven's voice reads the eviction as victory: salvation, power, the kingdom, and the authority of his Christ have come, and the conquerors conquered by the blood of the Lamb, the word of their testimony, and not loving their lives even to death.
16.question: Which of those three weapons is yours to take up this week?

16.title: The Dragon Went Off to Make War on the Rest
16.context: The dragon's short time is spent in pursuit: a river from his mouth, the earth opening its own mouth to swallow it, and then war on the rest of the woman's offspring, those who keep God's commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus.
16.question: Where has help come from an unexpected quarter when you were pursued?

17.title: A Beast Rising Out of the Sea
17.context: From the shore where the dragon stands, the war takes agents: a beast rising from the sea with ten horns, seven heads, ten crowns, and blasphemous names, like a leopard with a bear's feet and a lion's mouth, given the dragon's power, throne, and great authority.
17.question: What powers in your world borrow their authority from a source you should name honestly?

17.title: Who Is Like the Beast
17.context: One head bears a mortal wound that is healed, and the whole earth marvels and follows, worshiping the dragon for giving the beast its authority and asking the question that parodies heaven's own praise: who is like the beast?
17.question: What counterfeits of resurrection and wonder compete for your worship?

17.title: Authority for Forty-Two Months
17.context: The authority is real and leased, with a term: blasphemies for forty-two months, war on the saints, authority over every tribe and people, and the call that bounds it all, the perseverance and faith of the saints.
17.question: How does a known term on evil's lease change how you endure it?

17.title: A Second Beast, Like a Lamb, Speaking Like a Dragon
17.context: The second beast rises from the earth with two horns like a lamb and a dragon's speech, working the first beast's publicity: signs, fire from heaven, deception, an image that breathes and speaks, and death for those who will not worship it.
17.question: Where does lamb-like appearance hide dragon-like speech in your world?

17.title: The Number of a Man: 666
17.context: The enforcement reaches the marketplace: a mark on the right hand or forehead, without which no one can buy or sell. The chapter closes with a call for wisdom and the number as the book gives it, the number of a man, six hundred sixty-six. The telling computes no name.
17.question: What does it cost, in your ordinary buying and selling, to refuse the marks on offer?

18.title: The Lamb Standing on Mount Zion
18.context: Against the mark of the beast the vision sets a forehead of another kind: the Lamb standing on Mount Zion with the 144,000, his name and his Father's name written on their foreheads, singing a new song no one else could learn.
18.question: Whose name is written on your forehead, by the evidence of your week?

18.title: Fallen, Fallen Is Babylon the Great
18.context: Three angels cross mid-heaven with three announcements: an eternal gospel for every nation, fear God for the hour of judgment has come; and the first naming of the fall, Babylon the great is fallen, who made the nations drink her wine.
18.question: Where do you need to fear God more than the powers that announce themselves louder?

18.title: If Anyone Worships the Beast
18.context: The third angel speaks the severest speech in the book at full strength: worship of the beast and its image and its mark draws the wine of God's wrath, unmixed, with torment and no rest day or night. The telling softens none of it.
18.question: How do you hold a warning this severe together with the mercy you have received?

18.title: Blessed Are the Dead Who Die in the Lord
18.context: Immediately after the severest speech comes a blessing for the dying: write, blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on, and the Spirit answers yes, rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them.
18.question: What deeds of yours are worth having follow you?

18.title: Two Harvests
18.context: The chapter closes with two reapings swung like answers: the one like a son of man with a golden crown and a sharp sickle gathering the earth's ripe grain, and another angel gathering the clusters of the vine into the great winepress of God's wrath, trodden until blood flows.
18.question: What is ripening in your life, and toward which harvest?

19.title: A Sea of Glass Mixed with Fire
19.context: The last judgments are introduced as completion: seven angels with seven plagues, the last, because in them God's wrath is finished. Beside a sea of glass mixed with fire stand those who conquered the beast, holding God's harps.
19.question: Where do you need to stand and sing before the finish, not after it?

19.title: The Song of Moses and the Song of the Lamb
19.context: Their song carries two names, the song of God's servant Moses and the song of the Lamb, one song at the far shore as at the first: great and marvelous are your deeds, just and true your ways, King of the nations. All nations will come and worship.
19.question: What has God done in your life that deserves the word marvelous, said plainly?

19.title: The Sanctuary Filled with Smoke
19.context: Heaven's temple opens on the tabernacle of the Testimony; seven angels come out in pure bright linen with golden sashes, receive seven golden bowls full of wrath from one of the living creatures, and no one can enter the temple until the plagues finish.
19.question: What does it mean that even heaven waits, reverent, while wrath runs its course?

19.title: Go, Pour Out the Bowls
19.context: A loud voice from the temple gives the order, and the bowls go out in sequence: painful sores on the marked, the sea turned to blood until every living thing in it dies. The order and pace are the temple's, not the earth's.
19.question: Where do you need to let God's sequence stand instead of demanding your own?

19.title: You Are Just, O Holy One
19.context: At the third bowl, rivers and springs become blood, and the angel of the waters answers the judgment as justice: they shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink; they deserve it. Even the altar speaks: yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are your judgments.
19.question: Where do you need to call God's judgment just even when you cannot trace it?

19.title: They Did Not Repent and Give Him Glory
19.context: The fourth bowl scorches people with fire, and the fifth pours darkness on the beast's throne until people gnaw their tongues in anguish. Twice the refrain lands: they cursed God's name and did not repent.
19.question: What pain in your life is an unopened door to repentance?

20.title: The Kings of the Whole World Assembled
20.context: The sixth bowl dries the Euphrates into a road for the kings from the east, and three frog-like unclean spirits from the mouths of dragon, beast, and false prophet perform signs and go out to assemble the kings of the whole world for the great day's battle.
20.question: What assemblies in your world are being gathered by voices you should not follow?

20.title: Blessed Is the One Who Stays Awake
20.context: In the middle of the gathering the speaker interrupts his own vision with a beatitude: behold, I am coming like a thief; blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments. Then the place is named in Hebrew: Armageddon.
20.question: What does staying awake look like on an ordinary Tuesday?

20.title: It Is Done
20.context: The seventh bowl goes into the air and a loud voice from the throne declares: it is done. Lightning, thunder, and the greatest earthquake split the great city into three parts, and every island and mountain flees out of existence.
20.question: What in your life needs to hear it is done, in full, and stop being negotiated?

20.title: Hailstones Weighing Almost a Hundred Pounds
20.context: Last falls the hail, stones of almost a hundred pounds, and the chapter's last word on its targets is the refrain at its worst: they cursed God for the plague, because it was so severe.
20.question: When severity comes, will your reflex be curse or cry for mercy? What decides it?

21.title: Come, I Will Show You the Judgment of the Great Prostitute
21.context: One of the bowl angels pauses the action to explain a figure: the judgment of the great prostitute seated on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth committed sexual immorality and the earth's inhabitants were made drunk.
21.question: What intoxications in your world are sold as sophistication?

21.title: Seated on a Scarlet Beast
21.context: John is carried away in the Spirit into a wilderness and sees the woman seated on a scarlet beast full of blasphemous names, dressed in purple and scarlet and gold, holding a golden cup full of abominations, her forehead written with a mystery name, drunk with the blood of the saints.
21.question: What does the gold cup promise, and what does it actually hold?

21.title: Was, and Is Not, and Is About to Rise
21.context: The beast's biography is a riddle in three tenses: it was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction, and earth's inhabitants whose names are not in the book of life will marvel at it.
21.question: Whose marveling do you most need to refuse to join?

21.title: The Lamb Will Conquer Them
21.context: The angel interprets the anatomy: seven heads as mountains and kings, ten horns as ten kings who give their power to the beast for one hour and make war on the Lamb, who conquers them because he is Lord of lords and King of kings, with his called, chosen, and faithful ones beside him.
21.question: How does it steady you that the Lamb's victory is announced before the war chapter?

21.title: The Woman Is the Great City
21.context: Two of the angel's own glosses close the chapter and the telling uses them as given: the waters are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages, and the woman is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth. The beast and the horns will turn and devour their own rider.
21.question: What systems that promise glory end by devouring their own?

22.title: Fallen, Fallen Is Babylon the Great
22.context: An angel descends with such glory that the earth is lit by his splendor, and the announcement is finally made in public: fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, become a dwelling place for demons and a haunt for every unclean thing, because all nations drank her wine.
22.question: What glittering thing in your world is already fallen, whether or not the news has spread?

22.title: Come Out of Her, My People
22.context: Before the sentence falls, a second voice speaks the book's great rescue: come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins and share in her plagues. Her sins are heaped to heaven, and God remembers, paying back double and torment measured to her boasting.
22.question: What are you still inside of that this voice is calling you out of?

22.title: The Kings Who Will Weep and Wail
22.context: The chapter lets Babylon's mourners speak in her own tongue of trade. The kings who shared her luxury stand far off in fear of her torment, weeping over a city judged in a single hour.
22.question: Whose grief is real sorrow, and whose is only grief for lost luxury? How can you tell in yourself?

22.title: No One Buys Their Cargo Anymore
22.context: The merchants' lament is an inventory, the book's longest catalog: gold, silver, jewels, purple, silk, ivory, marble, spices, wine, oil, wheat, cattle, horses, chariots, and last and worst, slaves, that is, human souls.
22.question: What does a catalog ending in human souls say about every trade built on people?

22.title: All Who Had Ships Were Made Rich by Her
22.context: The sailors, every shipmaster and passenger and all who make their living by the sea, stand far off and throw dust on their heads over the wealth destroyed in one hour, while heaven and the saints are called to rejoice, because God has given judgment for them against her.
22.question: Where is heaven's rejoicing correcting your own first reaction?

22.title: So Will Babylon Be Thrown Down with Violence
22.context: A mighty angel seals the fall with an acted parable, hurling a millstone into the sea: so will Babylon be thrown down, and never found again. No music, no craftsman, no millstone's sound, no lamp, no wedding voice, and her merchants were the great ones of the earth.
22.question: What noise in your life would silence make holy?

23.title: Hallelujah: Salvation and Glory and Power
23.context: Babylon's fall is answered in heaven with the book's only hallelujahs, a great multitude's roar: salvation and glory and power belong to our God, for his judgments are true and just, and the twenty-four elders and four living creatures fall down with Amen, hallelujah.
23.question: What judgment of God could you learn to answer with hallelujah instead of questions?

23.title: The Marriage of the Lamb Has Come
23.context: The reign is celebrated as a wedding: let us rejoice and give him glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come and his bride has made herself ready, clothed in fine linen, bright and pure, which the verse itself names as the righteous deeds of the saints. Blessed are those invited to the marriage supper.
23.question: What righteous deed is your part of the bride making herself ready?

23.title: Worship God
23.context: John falls at the angel's feet and is corrected at once: you must not do that; I am a fellow servant. Worship God. For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy, the book's own definition, kept exactly.
23.question: Where do you need to refuse honor that belongs to God, quickly and plainly?

23.title: Faithful and True, on a White Horse
23.context: Heaven opens for the rider: a white horse, and its rider called Faithful and True, judging and making war in righteousness, eyes like flame, many crowns, a robe dipped in blood, armies in white linen behind him, and on his robe and thigh the name King of kings and Lord of lords.
23.question: Which of the rider's names do you need most to trust today?

23.title: Come, Gather for the Great Supper of God
23.context: An angel standing in the sun invites the birds to a grim opposite supper: the great supper of God, the flesh of kings and commanders and the mighty, of horses and riders, of all, free and slave, small and great, gathered for the battle Armageddon prepared.
23.question: How does a book that holds both suppers teach you the weight of invitations?

23.title: The Beast Was Captured
23.context: Then the war itself takes two verses: the beast is captured, and with it the false prophet who worked its signs, both thrown alive into the lake of fire, and the rest slain by the rider's sword, whose word does in a sentence what armies gathered chapters to attempt.
23.question: What battle are you arming for that his word could finish?

24.title: Bound for a Thousand Years
24.context: The dragon who started the war behind the war receives his own chain: an angel descends with the key to the bottomless pit and a great chain, seizes the ancient serpent, and binds him for a thousand years so he can deceive the nations no more, until the thousand years end and he must be released for a little while.
24.question: What deceiving voice do you most need to hear is bound, not sovereign?

24.title: Souls on Thrones, Reigning a Thousand Years
24.context: Then thrones, and authority to judge seated on them, and the souls of those beheaded for the testimony and for refusing the beast's worship and mark: they came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.
24.question: What does faithfulness cost in your world, and what reign is promised to it?

24.title: The First Resurrection
24.context: The book glosses its own event carefully: the rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years ended; this is the first resurrection, and blessed and holy is the one who shares in it, over whom the second death has no power. How the thousand years are read, as a future reign, a present one, or a symbol of Christ's victory, Christians have long disagreed; the chapter is told in its own sequence and no scheme is adopted. The reflection on that disagreement rides this scene.
24.question: How do you hold this chapter humbly, in its own order, without needing to win it?

25.title: Released to Deceive the Nations
25.context: The release announced in the binding arrives on schedule: when the thousand years end, Satan is released and goes out to deceive the nations at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, gathered for battle like the sand of the sea.
25.question: Where does an old deception return in your life wearing its final disguise?

25.title: Fire Came Down from Heaven
25.context: The last campaign is the shortest: they march up over the broad plain and surround the camp of the saints and the beloved city, fire comes down from heaven and consumes them, and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire where the beast and false prophet already are, tormented day and night forever.
25.question: What surrounded thing in your life needs heaven's fire rather than your strategy?

25.title: A Great White Throne
25.context: Then the last sight of the old order: a great white throne and the one seated on it, from whose presence earth and sky flee away, and no place is found for them. Every other throne in the book has led to this one.
25.question: What would you stop hiding if you believed no place hides from that presence?

25.title: Judged by What Was Written in the Books
25.context: Every hiding place for the dead is emptied: sea, death, and Hades give them up, the books are opened, and another book, the book of life. The dead are judged by what was written, according to their deeds, and death and Hades themselves are thrown into the lake of fire, the second death.
25.question: What does it mean for you that the book of life, not only the books of deeds, is open at the end?

26.title: A New Heaven and a New Earth
26.context: Then a new heaven and a new earth, the first ones passed away and the sea no more, and the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.
26.question: What would you build differently if the end were renewal, not escape?

26.title: He Will Wipe Away Every Tear
26.context: A loud voice from the throne announces the book's thesis: behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and he will wipe every tear, and death and mourning and crying and pain will be no more, for the former things have passed away.
26.question: Which former thing do you most long to watch pass away?

26.title: Behold, I Make All Things New
26.context: The one seated on the throne speaks in his own person: behold, I make all things new; write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true. It is done; I am the Alpha and the Omega, and to the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment. The framing reflection rides this scene.
26.question: Where is he making things new that you have only been able to see as loss?

26.title: The Cowardly, the Faithless, the Detestable
26.context: The same voice contains the book's last severity, at full strength: the cowardly, the faithless, the detestable, murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars have their portion in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, the second death. Nothing in the new creation is built on pretending.
26.question: Which item on that list most calls you to honesty rather than fear?

27.title: Twelve Gates, Twelve Tribes
27.context: One of the bowl angels returns with a different errand: come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb. Carried to a great high mountain, John sees the city descending, radiant, with twelve gates named for the tribes and twelve foundations named for the apostles.
27.question: How does the city honoring both covenants change how you read your own place in the story?

27.title: Measured with a Golden Rod
27.context: The angel measures with a golden rod: a cube of twelve thousand stadia, its wall of jasper, its foundations layered in jewels, its twelve gates single pearls, its street pure gold like transparent glass. The reflection on the city as memory and measurement rides this scene.
27.question: What does a measured, jewel-founded permanence promise your temporary life?

27.title: The Glory of God Gives It Light
27.context: The absences define the city: no temple, for its temple is the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb; no sun or moon, for God's glory is its light and the Lamb its lamp; no night, no shut gates, nothing unclean, only those written in the Lamb's book of life.
27.question: Which absence in the city do you find yourself longing for most?

27.title: The River of the Water of Life
27.context: Inside, Eden runs through the city like a river: the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne down the middle of the street, the tree of life on either side bearing twelve kinds of fruit monthly, its leaves for the healing of the nations, and no curse anymore, forever.
27.question: What healing of the nations, or of your own house, do you want to ask for by name?

28.title: These Words Are Trustworthy and True
28.context: The book closes by certifying itself: these words are trustworthy and true, and the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place. The first beatitude of the ending: blessed is the one who keeps the words of this prophecy.
28.question: Which word from this book are you resolved to keep, in one concrete practice?

28.title: Worship God, Again
28.context: John, for the second time, falls at the angel's feet and is corrected in the same words: you must not do that; I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep this book's words. Worship God.
28.question: What repeated mistake of yours needs a repeated, patient correction?

28.title: Do Not Seal Up the Words of This Prophecy
28.context: Against Daniel, told to seal his book until the time of the end, John is told the opposite: do not seal up the words, for the time is near. The book is left open on purpose, its invitation standing in the open air.
28.question: What truth have you been sealing that was given to you open?

28.title: Blessed Are Those Who Wash Their Robes
28.context: The coming is announced once more with its justice: behold, I am coming soon, bringing my recompense. And the book's last blessing falls on those who wash their robes, in the BSB's wording, who have the right to the tree of life and enter the city by its gates, while outside remains the exclusion the book does not hide.
28.question: What washing do you need before you can enter by the gates gladly?

28.title: I, Jesus, Have Sent My Angel
28.context: Then Jesus signs the book in his own voice, the only signature of its kind in the whole work: I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you about these things for the churches. I am the Root and the Descendant of David, the bright morning star.
28.question: What does it change that the book's last signature is his, not the seer's?

28.title: Let the One Who Is Thirsty Come
28.context: The warning stands guard over the whole invitation: the Spirit and the bride say come, and whoever takes away from this prophecy loses his share in the tree of life. Let the one who hears say come, and let the thirsty take the water of life without price.
28.question: Who needs to hear come from you this week, in the Spirit's voice rather than your own pressure?

28.title: Amen. Come, Lord Jesus
28.context: The last exchange the whole book was traveling toward: he who testifies says, yes, I am coming soon, and the church answers what it has learned to say, amen, come, Lord Jesus. The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints, and the book ends where the letters began, in grace.
28.question: What would it mean for your prayers to end, more often, with come?
